hints: Look closely at the stage names and picture what each chromosome looks like: in early prophase and metaphase each chromosome is still made of two sister chromatids joined together, but what happens to that join in anaphase?

Remember the golden rule: 1 chromosome = 1 centromere, even if that chromosome has 2 chromatids. Count how many separate chromosomes (and therefore centromeres) exist before and after the sisters split apart.
walkthrough:
**Recall what a centromere is**

Think of the centromere as the button that holds two sister chromatids together to make one chromosome.

So the rule is simple:
$$1 \text{ chromosome} = 1 \text{ centromere}$$

**Count centromeres in early prophase and metaphase**

A human muscle cell is diploid with 46 chromosomes. By early prophase, DNA has replicated, so each of the 46 chromosomes now consists of two chromatids, but they are still joined by one centromere each.

In metaphase they line up on the equator, but they have not split yet. So we still have:
$$46 \text{ chromosomes} = 46 \text{ centromeres}$$

**Count centromeres in anaphase**

Anaphase is the splitting moment. The centromeres divide and the sister chromatids are pulled apart. Each chromatid now becomes an independent chromosome, each with its own centromere.

So the number doubles:
$$46 \times 2 = 92 \text{ centromeres}$$
That gives 46, 46, 92, which is option A.

options.A: Correct. 46 centromeres in early prophase and metaphase (one per double-chromatid chromosome), doubling to 92 in anaphase when sister chromatids separate.
options.B: Incorrect. Metaphase still has 46 centromeres, not 92, because the sister chromatids have lined up but have not yet split.
options.C: Incorrect. Anaphase cannot stay at 46, because splitting of centromeres creates twice as many separate chromosomes and centromeres.
options.D: Incorrect. Early prophase does not have 92 centromeres. DNA replication doubles chromatids and DNA, but not the number of centromeres or chromosomes.
